analysis.one_liner: Bars debt collectors from texting or emailing people without their consent.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill 31-23 in March 2020, but it never received a vote by the full House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal debt collection law so a collector cannot email or text you without your consent, cannot keep contacting you after you withdraw consent, and cannot contact you more often than you agreed to. It also stops the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau from writing rules that let collectors send unlimited emails and texts, requires collectors to let you opt out of any contact method, and orders the bureau to report yearly on consumer complaints about collectors' electronic messages and on its enforcement actions against collectors.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly one in three adults with debt in collections benefits: the bill would give them control over whether a collector can reach them by email or text, how often, and the ability to say stop at any time, while adding public reports on complaints and enforcement.

how_it_helps.text: It makes electronic contact without a consumer's consent a form of harassment under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, including contact after consent is withdrawn or more often than the consumer agreed to.

It forbids the CFPB from issuing any debt collection rule that allows collectors to send unlimited emails and texts to a consumer, at a time when the bureau was writing a rule that would permit routine electronic contact.
It requires collectors to get consent directly from the consumer before using any method other than mail or phone, and lets consumers opt out of any contact method at any time.
It orders the CFPB and the FTC to report publicly on debt collection complaints, including a state-by-state breakdown, and on enforcement actions taken against debt collectors.

analysis.who_pays: Debt collection agencies and debt buyers bear the cost: they could no longer blast consumers with texts and emails by default and would need affirmative consent for electronic contact, which makes reaching debtors cheaper and faster.

drawbacks.text: Restricting electronic contact makes collections slower and more expensive, and collectors may pass some of that cost on to other consumers through higher fees or by selling debts.
Requiring consent before any email or text could cut off a channel some consumers actually prefer, leaving only mail and phone calls that many people screen or ignore.
The added semi-annual and annual reporting requirements impose administrative work on the CFPB, FTC, and debt collection firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are modest but real: they hand control of electronic contact back to the person being contacted and prevent a rule that would have allowed unlimited texts and emails. The cost falls on collection firms rather than taxpayers, and the main downside is slower or costlier collection efforts, which matters most to consumers who want to resolve debts quickly and to collectors' bottom lines. The bill does not change what is owed or wipe out any debt.

outcome.mechanism: The Financial Services Committee approved it 31-23 and it was placed on the House calendar in March 2020, but House leaders never scheduled a floor vote before the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the bill on November 8, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The committee marked up the bill on November 13-14, 2019, and ordered it reported as amended by a vote of 31 to 23.
Eight Democratic representatives added their names as cosponsors when the bill was reported in March 2020.
On March 19, 2020, the committee reported the bill as amended and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the queue of bills awaiting House floor action.
No floor vote ever came, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection agencies came out ahead: without the bill becoming law, collectors kept the ability to contact people by email and text without consent and faced no statutory bar on unlimited electronic messages, and the CFPB's rulemaking was not constrained by the bill's limits.

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through committee markup.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill over two days and approved it as amended, 31-23, reporting it to the House floor in March 2020.

for.name: 8 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as additional sponsors when the bill was reported.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Decides which bills on the calendar get floor time
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote after it was placed on the Union Calendar; the bill died there at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote of 31-23 suggests most Democrats supported reporting the bill and most Republicans opposed it, but the record does not break down that roll call by party, and the House never voted on final passage.

industries.industry: Debt collection agencies and debt buyers
industries.note: The bill would have required collectors to get a consumer's consent before emailing or texting them and would have banned rules allowing unlimited electronic messages, cutting off their cheapest, highest-volume contact channel. Ordinary people with debts in collections would have gained control over when and how collectors reach them.

The bill would have constrained the bureau's pending debt collection rulemaking, barring any rule that permits unlimited emails and texts, while also assigning it new public reporting duties on complaints and enforcement.
